subtype: Approach: shouts out many ideas together before choosing one [Thinking]
passage: In a kindergarten in Singapore, a week before Diwali, the teacher asked, 'How can we decorate our classroom?' Hands shot up and voices tumbled: 'Flowers!' 'Lamps!' 'Paper chains!' 'Rangoli!' Hana shouted, 'Stars!' and Mina yelled, 'Lots of flowers!' The teacher wrote every idea on a big sheet and said no to none. When the shouting stopped, there were nine ideas. Then the teacher said, 'Everyone gets two stickers.' The children stuck them beside their favourites. Paper chains and lamps got the most. Hana clapped. 'Stars can come next time,' said the teacher.

qa.q: How many ideas did the teacher write on the sheet?
qa.a: The teacher wrote nine ideas on the sheet.

qa.q: How did Hana seem to feel when the stickers were counted?
qa.a: Hana seemed happy and fine about it, clapping for paper chains and lamps even though stars did not win.

qa.q: What could the class do so that Hana's idea is not left out?
qa.a: The class could hang a few paper stars on the paper chains, since a small piece of a favourite idea can fit with the chosen ones.

qa.q: How might the teacher have felt while listening to all the shouting?
qa.a: The teacher was probably pleased and amused to see the children so full of ideas, since every idea was written down. 🙂

grounding: Shows children calling out many ideas for festival decorations together, the teacher writing all of them, and the class then voting for two.

subtype: Approach: shouts out many ideas together before choosing one [Thinking]
passage:
In the KG classroom, Hemant Sir held up a marker. "Diwali is coming! How shall we decorate our room?"
Hands shot up. "Flowers!" "Lamps!" "Paper chains!" "Rangoli!" "Balloons!" Sumit jumped up. "Stars on the window!"
Sir wrote every idea on the board, even the funny one about painting the fan.
Then he said, "Now we choose two. Put your hand up for your favourite."
Sumit voted for stars. Most children chose lamps and paper chains.
Sumit's lip wobbled. Hemant Sir smiled at him. "Stars can go on the door next week."
He clapped.

qa.q: Which two ideas did most children choose?
qa.a: Most children chose lamps and paper chains.

qa.q: How did Sumit feel when stars did not win?
qa.a: He felt sad and disappointed, which is why his lip wobbled.

qa.q: What else could the teacher try so more children feel their idea was used?
qa.a: Hemant Sir could keep the list and use a different idea each week, so ideas that lose the vote still get a turn.

qa.q: How might the children feel about Hemant Sir writing every idea on the board?
qa.a: They may feel happy and listened to, since even the funny idea about painting the fan went up on the board.

grounding: It shows young children calling out many ideas for decorating the classroom while the teacher writes them all, and then the class votes for two.

subtype: Approach: shouts out many ideas together before choosing one [Thinking]
passage:
I'm Raghav from Class 8. On Fridays I help in the Class 1 room.
Last week their teacher asked how to decorate for Pongal. Nandini, the smallest girl, shouted "Kolam!" first. Then everyone: "Sugarcane!" "Pots!" "Mango leaves!" "Kites!"
The teacher didn't say yes or no. She just wrote every word on the board, with little drawings.
Then she said, "Now let's pick two." Hands went up. Kolam and mango leaves won.
Nandini jumped up and down. Maybe she felt proud, but I can't say for sure. She drew a huge chalk kolam by the door.

qa.q: Which two ideas won the vote?
What might Nandini's jumping up and down suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt excited and proud that her idea won, though Raghav can't say for sure.

qa.q: What else could the teacher do with the ideas that did not win?
qa.a: She could save them for the next festival, so every child's idea still feels valued.

qa.q: How might the other children see the teacher writing every word without saying yes or no?
qa.a: They may feel safe to call out any idea, since nothing was judged until the vote.

grounding: It shows young children calling out many decoration ideas, the teacher writing all of them first, and then a class vote picking two.
